newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Coceral sees record EU grain crop.
newsitem.headline: Coceral sees record EU grain crop.

text.p: The European Union grain trade group forecast on Friday a record EU crop of 201 million tonnes, 25 million tonnes more than last year's harvest after farmers expanded plantings and favourable weather helped boost yields.
COCERAL, which represents grain traders in the 15 member states, raised its forecast for grain production from 198.5 million in September after wheat and maize figures were adjusted upwards.
The previous record was in 1991 when the EU produced 182.6 million tonnes. The figure includes Swedish, Finnish and Austria output although they only joined the EU in 1995.
"The final figure after the maize harvest is finished could be even higher," a trade source said, adding prices would continue to fall under pressure from the massive crop.

Farmers took advantage of high world prices last year and an easing of EU planting restrictions to expand the cereals area by five percent while yields shot up nearly 10 percent compared with last year's drought damaged crop.

European Commission grain officials, who last month poured cold water over figures pointing to a breakthrough of the 200-million tonnes barrier, did not comment on the new forecast at a meeting with grain traders on Friday.
Instead they urged farmers to release grain onto domestic markets so as to bring prices down to more competitive international levels.
Trade delegates at the meeting complained that EU grain exports were lagging far behind U.S. shipments.

But the Commission warned of only limited funds available for subsidising exports of expensive EU grain. It said that barley export subsidies were already nearly $40 a tonne and could not continue to climb.
A lot of this year's extra grain is poor quality wheat, suitable for farm animals, which will have to be exported with subsidies.
"This will annoy the Americans because it competes with their maize exports," another trade source said.

U.S. Department of Agriculture officials warned the EU's executive Commission during talks in Brussels this week against raising wheat export subsidies and renewing the grain subsidy war of the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Meanwhile, the USDA cut its U.S. wheat production estimate to 2.282 bushels from 2.295 billion in September and revised downward its 1996-97 ending stocks estimate to 470 million from 506 million in September.
In its latest forecast, COCERAL put the maize harvest, which is not yet complete, 14 percent higher than last year at 33.3 million tonnes. Maize is used mainly to feed farm animals.

Bread-making wheat is seen 12 percent higher at 90.2 million tonnes, barley 19 percent up at 52.3 million and durum wheat, used for pasta and biscuits, is seen jumping 34 percent to 7.6 million tonnes.
The balance is made up of rye, sorghum, oats and other grains used mainly to feed animals.
